notes.meaning: Seven full days of setting Aaron and his sons apart for God have now ended. On this eighth day, Moses calls the priests and Israel's elders together so the priests can start their regular work. The elders attend as leaders to represent the whole nation and see Aaron take up his duties.

Moses tells Aaron to bring a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, each without any physical flaw. Even after a week of dedication at the tabernacle, Aaron still has personal sins that need to be cleared before God. Many ancient teachers note that a calf was chosen to remind Aaron of his past failure with the golden calf.

Aaron is instructed to tell the Israelites to bring their own collection of animals for sacrifice. These include a goat for a sin offering, a calf and lamb for a burnt offering, an ox and ram for a peace offering, and grain mixed with oil. Moses explains the wonderful reason for these gifts: the Lord Himself will appear to the people on this day.

differ.view: The order of these sacrifices pictures the steps of salvation: first pardon for sin, then total dedication to God, and finally peaceful fellowship with Him.

notes.meaning: The people promptly bring every animal and gift that Moses asked for to the front of the sacred tent. The whole assembly gathers in the courtyard and stands reverently in God's presence. Their shared obedience shows that the entire nation is eager to meet with the Lord.

Moses reminds the crowd that following God's exact commands prepares the way for His presence. When they carry out these duties in faith, God's glory—a visible display of His royal majesty and power—will be revealed among them. Obedience to God's word always comes before the display of His glory.

Moses directs Aaron to step up to the altar and offer sacrifices to make atonement, which means making things right between God and sinners. Aaron must offer a sacrifice for himself first, and only then for the people. This order shows that human priests are imperfect sinners who need forgiveness before they can help anyone else.

Aaron obeys Moses and goes directly to the bronze altar to kill the calf for his own sin offering. By killing the animal with his own hands, he openly confesses that he is a sinner in need of mercy. This act sets an example of humble honesty before the people he is called to lead.

Aaron's sons catch the blood in a basin and bring it to their father at the altar. Aaron dips his finger into the blood, smears it on the four raised corners of the altar, and pours out the rest at the altar's base. Because he has not yet entered the inner sanctuary, the blood is applied only to the outside altar in the courtyard.

Aaron places the best fat pieces, the kidneys, and the liver lobe on the altar fire as the Lord commanded. He takes the rest of the meat and hide and burns them completely outside the camp. Because this offering is for the priest himself, he is not permitted to eat any of the meat.

Aaron next kills the ram for his burnt offering, an animal given entirely to God as a sign of complete surrender. His sons hand him the blood, and he splashes it against all sides of the altar. This follows the pattern given earlier for whole burnt sacrifices.

The sons bring the ram to Aaron piece by piece, including the head, and he lays them on the altar. He washes the inner parts and the legs with water to clean them before burning them on top of the other pieces. The careful handling of each part shows deep reverence, with nothing rushed or treated as ordinary.

Now that Aaron has made atonement for himself, he can act on behalf of the nation. He takes the male goat brought for the people's sin offering, kills it, and presents it just as he did his own sacrifice. His personal cleansing has prepared him to serve his neighbors.

Aaron brings forward the calf and lamb that the people provided for their burnt offering. He sacrifices them according to the rules God had set down in earlier laws. Carrying out each step by the book establishes a faithful pattern for Israel's future worship.

Aaron presents the grain offering made of fine flour and oil, scoops up a handful, and burns it on the altar. This special gift is placed on the altar in addition to the regular lamb offered every morning. God's special celebrations do not replace the faithful daily worship He requires.

Aaron slaughters the ox and ram for the people's peace offering, which celebrates friendship and harmony with God. His sons bring him the blood, and he splashes it against every side of the altar. This sacrifice provides meat for a joyful community meal once peace with God is secured.

The priests gather the fat portions of the ox and ram, including the broad tail, the fat covering the organs, and the kidneys. They place these rich portions on the animal breasts and carry them to the altar. Aaron burns the fat on the fire because the richest part belongs to God alone.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the mention of waving the right thigh was copied from Leviticus 7, because elsewhere the right thigh is usually lifted up as a contribution rather than waved.

notes.meaning: Aaron lifts up the breasts and the right thighs and waves them back and forth before the Lord. This wave offering presents the food to God as owner of all things, and He then gives these choice cuts back to the priests to support them. Moses had commanded this practice so the priests would have food for their families.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think mentioning the right thigh as a waved offering here may be a later editorial note, since earlier rules describe the breast as waved and the thigh as lifted up.

notes.meaning: With the sacrifices completed, Aaron lifts his hands from the altar platform and speaks a blessing over the assembled people. He then steps down from the raised ramp of the altar. The blessing shows that God's favor and peace flow freely once sin has been covered.

Moses leads Aaron inside the tent of meeting to show him the sacred duties at the lampstand, table, and incense altar. When they come out, both leaders bless the people together. At that moment, the radiant glory of the Lord appears in plain sight of the entire congregation.

Supernatural fire flashes from God's presence and instantly burns up the sacrifices on the altar. This miracle proves that God has accepted Aaron's priesthood and forgiven the nation's sins. Seeing this, the people shout for joy and fall facedown in holy awe.

differ.view: The heavenly fire represents the Holy Spirit entering believers' hearts to burn away sin and inspire pure love for God.
The descent of divine fire shows that proper rituals and forms are never enough without a direct, supernatural outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
